structure.title: Module 13: Conversation UI
structure.prefix_summary:
# Module 13: Conversation UI

Module 13 is the primary interface that sales reps interact with during every customer engagement. It is a real-time, state-driven application that reflects the current session’s context, active agent, discovery progress, and recommendations. Every visual element on screen is a function of the session state held in Module 1 (State Engine) and pushed to the UI via WebSocket.

nodes.title: 13.1 Layout Architecture
nodes.prefix_summary:
The document describes the layout architecture of a Conversation UI designed as a multi-panel, guided-selling workspace rather than a simple chat interface. It explains that the interface is composed of six clearly defined components, each with a specific screen position, purpose, and primary data source.

The Chat Panel serves as the central area for conversation between the sales representative and the AI assistant, powered by the state engine and orchestrator. The Customer Context Panel provides account details, product usage, and health metrics, pulling data from CRM/ERP integrations and session state. Discovery Progress visually tracks completion across sales discovery dimensions using configuration and state data. The Recommendations Panel presents product or solution suggestions with supporting reasoning, drawing from orchestration logic, knowledge base data, and feedback scoring. The Quick Actions Bar offers dynamic, context-sensitive buttons triggered by plugins and state conditions. Finally, the Agent Indicator displays the currently active workflow agent and supports transitions between agents.

Overall, the section outlines how the UI integrates multiple backend modules into a cohesive, real-time sales guidance environment.

nodes.title: 13.1.1 Chat Panel — The Conversation Thread
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Chat Panel**, which serves as the central conversation interface between the sales representative and the AI assistant.

It explains that the Chat Panel displays messages in chronological order with clear visual differentiation between rep and AI messages. AI responses are structured outputs generated by the currently active agent in Module 2, rather than free-form text. These responses may include embedded interactive elements such as inline product links (connected to the Recommendations Panel), discovery questions (which update Discovery Progress when answered), and action suggestions (linked to Quick Action buttons).

The section also outlines how the Chat Panel integrates with the system’s session state. It subscribes to the `conversation_history` layer in Module 1 and updates in real time when a `state_changed` event is broadcast by the State Engine.

Finally, it details the message rendering pipeline: from the rep submitting a message, through backend processing and agent orchestration, to the structured response being appended and pushed via WebSocket to the UI. The system targets sub-2-second latency, with a typing indicator displayed during longer processing tasks.

nodes.title: 13.1.2 Customer Context Panel
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Customer Context Panel**, a read-only sidebar in the Conversation UI that provides sales reps with a comprehensive view of all relevant customer information before and during a conversation.

The panel is populated at the start of a session when Module M1 gathers initial context by calling Module M4 (Data Integration) to retrieve CRM and ERP data. It serves as a reference surface and cannot be edited by the representative during the session.

The panel includes the following sections:

- **Account Header:** Company details such as name, industry, segment, and account owner (sourced from CRM).
- **Current Products:** Active subscriptions, contract dates, and usage levels (from ERP).
- **Key Metrics:** Business performance indicators like ARR, growth rate, NPS, and support ticket volume (from CRM and ERP).
- **Health Score:** A composite metric derived from usage, support, and payment signals, computed by M4 and M16, with potential real-time updates if CRM signals change mid-session.
- **Recent Activity:** The last five customer touchpoints, including calls, emails, meetings, and support cases.
- **Relationship Map:** Key contacts, their roles, and decision-making authority within the account.

Most data updates at session start, except for the Health Score, which can update in real time if underlying signals change.

The section also explains why the panel is read-only: allowing edits within the Conversation UI could create synchronization conflicts with the CRM system. Instead, all CRM write-backs occur through a dedicated CRM Widget (Module 14), where the CRM remains the system of record. The Conversation UI is designed to support selling activities, not data entry.

nodes.title: 13.1.3 Discovery Progress
nodes.summary:
The partial document describes the **Discovery Progress** component, which tracks and visualizes how effectively a sales representative has uncovered a customer’s needs across multiple defined dimensions.

The system organizes discovery into named categories (such as Business Challenges, Infrastructure, Timeline, and Budget), each represented by a progress percentage from 0–100%. As conversations progress and relevant information is identified, the active agent automatically updates the corresponding dimension’s progress through a system call. These updates are pushed to the user interface in real time via WebSocket, where progress bars animate accordingly.

In the MVP version, the system uses a fixed set of five standard dimensions with equal weighting. Progress increases in a binary way—when a required question is answered, the related dimension advances. Discovery is considered complete when all dimensions reach at least 80%.

In the full product, the system becomes highly customizable. Discovery dimensions are configurable per tenant through an Admin Portal, with settings stored in a multi-tenancy configuration module. Dimensions can have different weights, progress increments are based on the depth and quality of responses (not just binary completion), visualization is upgraded to a radar/spider chart with color coding, and completion thresholds can be configured per tenant and workflow.

nodes.title: 13.1.4 Recommendations Panel
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Recommendations Panel**, the user interface component where the platform’s intelligent product suggestions are presented to the sales representative.

When an agent in M2 determines a suitable product or solution, it generates a structured recommendation object. This object is stored in M1’s session state and delivered to the UI via WebSocket. Each recommendation appears as a card containing the product name, a confidence score, a natural-language explanation of the reasoning, supporting evidence from the knowledge base or CRM, and action buttons: **Accept**, **Dismiss**, and **Learn More**.

User interactions drive system behavior. Clicking **Accept** moves the product into the **Accepted Products Tray**, while **Dismiss** sends feedback to M16 (the Feedback Engine). 

The **Accepted Products Tray** is a persistent sub-component that tracks products selected during the session. Its contents are stored in M1’s `accepted_products` state layer and are accessible to all agents. Accepted products influence future recommendations—for example, selecting a UCaaS product prompts cross-sell agents to suggest complementary offerings rather than competing ones.

nodes.title: 13.1.5 Quick Actions Bar
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Quick Actions Bar**, a dynamic UI component that displays interactive buttons generated by the Plugin SDK (M12). The bar updates in real time based on conversation context: buttons appear when a plugin’s `triggerConditions` are met and disappear when they are no longer satisfied. It listens to M12’s plugin trigger evaluations to control visibility.

When a representative clicks a Quick Action button, the system sends an execution request to M12’s Plugin Gateway. The plugin runs in a sandboxed environment, accesses platform APIs (such as state, knowledge base, and conversation history), generates output using standardized UI templates (Card, Table, Form, or Custom Component), and renders the result in a Side Panel—without requiring the rep to leave the main interface.

The section also defines button states and their visual treatments:
- **Visible + Active:** Fully functional when trigger conditions are met; may include emphasis for high-priority suggestions.
- **Visible + Disabled:** Displayed but inactive when partial conditions are met, with a tooltip explaining missing requirements.
- **Hidden:** Not rendered when conditions are unmet or the plugin is disabled.
- **Loading:** Shows a spinner while execution is in progress.
- **Error:** Displays a red border and retry option if execution fails after exceeding circuit breaker limits.

Overall, the section outlines the dynamic behavior, execution flow, and UI state management of the Quick Actions Bar.

nodes.title: 13.1.6 Agent Indicator
nodes.summary:
### 13.1.6 Agent Indicator

The Agent Indicator is a small but critical UI element that shows which workflow agent (M6–M11) is currently active. It displays as a badge in the top bar with the agent’s name and icon (e.g., “Cross-Sell” with a branching icon, “Renewal” with a refresh icon). When the Orchestrator in M2 detects that a different agent should take over (based on trigger conditions and conversation flow), the Agent Indicator shows a subtle animation and a “Suggested switch” tooltip. The rep can accept or dismiss the switch suggestion.

This element reinforces the “rep in control” principle: the platform never silently switches agents. The rep always sees what’s happening and can override. The agent transition is logged in M1’s state as an agent_transition event, which M16 (Feedback Engine) uses to track whether agent switches correlate with better outcomes.

nodes.title: 13.2 Real-Time Communication — WebSocket Protocol
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 13.2 Real-Time Communication — WebSocket Protocol

Module 13 is the only interface module that communicates primarily via WebSocket rather than REST API. This is a deliberate architectural choice: the Conversation UI needs sub-second updates for typing indicators, state changes, recommendation arrivals, and agent transitions. REST polling would introduce unacceptable latency and unnecessary load.

nodes.title: 13.2.1 Connection Lifecycle
nodes.summary:
This section describes the full WebSocket-based connection lifecycle for a representative using the Conversation UI.

It begins with the **Connect** phase, where the client initiates a secure WebSocket connection using a JWT token. The authentication module validates the token and extracts tenant and user identifiers.

During **Authenticate**, the server binds the socket to a session. Existing sessions for the same account can be resumed, ensuring continuity.

In the **Subscribe** phase, the client subscribes to specific communication channels such as conversation updates, state changes, recommendations, plugins, and agent interactions. The server confirms these subscriptions.

Once **Active**, bidirectional communication occurs: the client sends messages and actions, while the server pushes state updates, AI agent responses, recommendations, and plugin events.

A **Heartbeat** mechanism maintains connection health, with periodic ping/pong messages. Missing three heartbeats triggers server-side cleanup.

Finally, on **Disconnect**, the server persists the session state to warm storage (PostgreSQL). Sessions remain resumable for up to 24 hours.

nodes.title: 13.2.2 Message Types — Server to Client
nodes.summary:
This section defines the **Server-to-Client message types** used in the system’s real-time communication layer and explains how each message affects the user interface.

### Main Points Covered

1. **Structured Message Framework**
   - Each server message includes a defined **message type**, a structured **payload**, and a corresponding **UI action**.
   - This ensures consistent synchronization between backend state changes and frontend updates.

2. **State and Data Synchronization**
   - **`state_changed`**: Updates specific UI panels (e.g., Context, Discovery) using deltas and version numbers to support optimistic UI conflict resolution.
   - **`discovery_updated`**: Updates progress indicators and highlights the triggering discovery input.

3. **Chat and Communication Updates**
   - **`message_appended`**: Adds assistant messages to the Chat Panel, including structured metadata (embedded actions, product mentions, discovery updates).
   - **`typing_indicator`**: Displays or hides typing indicators while the agent is processing.

4. **Recommendations and Insights**
   - **`recommendation_surfaced`**: Displays recommendation cards in the Recommendations Panel, sorted by confidence and supported by reasoning and evidence.

5. **Plugin System Interactions**
   - **`plugin_triggered`**: Adds plugin actions to a Quick Actions Bar based on priority.
   - **`plugin_result`**: Opens a Side Panel and renders plugin output using predefined templates (Card, Table, Form, Custom).

6. **Agent Workflow Management**
   - **`agent_transition`**: Updates the UI when switching between agents, optionally prompting user confirmation if the transition is suggested.

7. **Error Handling**
   - **`error`**: Displays toast notifications with optional recovery instructions (e.g., session reload if non-recoverable).

Overall, the section outlines how different server-originated events drive dynamic UI updates, ensuring real-time responsiveness, structured interaction flows, plugin extensibility, recommendation surfacing, and robust error handling.

nodes.title: 13.2.3 Message Types — Client to Server
nodes.summary:
The document section outlines the **client-to-server WebSocket message types** used in a real-time conversation system and explains why WebSockets are preferred over REST for this use case.

### Main Points Covered:

1. **Client-to-Server Message Types and Backend Actions**
   - **send_message**: Adds a user message to conversation history, routes it to the active agent, processes it, and returns the response.
   - **accept_recommendation**: Moves a recommended product to an accepted state, records the acceptance signal, and notifies agents.
   - **dismiss_recommendation**: Records dismissal (optionally with a reason), hides the recommendation, and updates agent behavior.
   - **execute_plugin**: Triggers a plugin through a sandboxed Plugin Gateway and returns the result.
   - **accept_agent_switch**: Switches the active agent, logs the transition, and updates the UI indicator.
   - **dismiss_agent_switch**: Suppresses the suggested agent switch for the session and records the dismissal.
   - **feedback_signal**: Records structured feedback (e.g., thumbs up/down, edits) for analytics and learning.

2. **Architectural Rationale for WebSockets over REST**
   - The Conversation UI generates frequent state updates (10–20 per minute per session).
   - REST polling would create significant overhead due to repeated HTTP requests, authentication parsing, and serialization.
   - WebSockets maintain a persistent connection, enabling lightweight real-time updates.
   - At scale (e.g., 500 concurrent users), WebSockets drastically reduce request volume and infrastructure load.
   - Enables true real-time server push instead of client polling intervals.

Overall, the section defines real-time messaging contracts between client and server and justifies the architectural choice of WebSockets for performance and scalability.

nodes.title: 13.3 State-Driven UI Rendering
nodes.summary:
This section explains that the UI in Module 13 is entirely state-driven and acts as a projection of M1’s persisted session state. The UI does not maintain independent local state; instead, every visual component reconstructs from the central session state, ensuring that refreshing the page does not cause data loss.

It maps each UI component to specific layers and fields within M1’s session state, including:
- Chat Panel tied to conversation history.
- Customer Context Panel tied to customer context data.
- Discovery Progress tied to discovery tracking fields.
- Recommendations Panel tied to recommendation state.
- Quick Actions Bar tied to plugin state.
- Agent Indicator tied to agent state and transitions.

The section also describes the synchronization model:
- On connection, the UI performs a full state sync via an API call that retrieves the complete session state snapshot.
- After initialization, updates are delivered incrementally through WebSocket as state deltas to improve responsiveness and reduce bandwidth usage.

Finally, it details optimistic UI behavior and conflict resolution:
- User actions (like sending a message) are rendered immediately as pending.
- Server confirmations update the state and clear pending markers.
- If rejected, the UI rolls back changes and shows an error.
- Version numbers in state updates ensure consistency; mismatched versions trigger a full state re-sync.

nodes.title: 13.4 UX Principles — How They Translate to Code
nodes.summary:
The document explains how four core UX principles—Dynamic, Rep in Control, Progressive Disclosure, and Workflow Aware—are concretely implemented in the system’s code and interface behavior.

**Dynamic** means UI elements (like Quick Action buttons) appear or disappear based on real-time session state. This is achieved through trigger evaluations tied to session conditions, with conditional rendering and automatic removal via DOM transitions when conditions change.

**Rep in Control** ensures that AI only suggests actions, never enforces them. All recommendations require explicit Accept/Dismiss input from the representative. Agent switches are optional, plugin outputs are shown for review in a side panel, and no automated execution occurs without user action. User choices are tracked to improve future recommendations.

**Progressive Disclosure** reduces cognitive load by showing only essential information upfront and loading additional details on demand. Core customer context appears at session start, while deeper product, competitive, or historical insights are fetched when requested or when deemed relevant by contextual logic.

**Workflow Aware** ensures the interface adapts to the currently active agent. Visual cues (badges, colors, response styling) change per agent, and available quick actions are filtered to match the agent’s workflow. Discovery priorities may also adjust dynamically based on the active agent context.

nodes.title: 13.5 Session Lifecycle from the UI Perspective
nodes.summary:
This section explains the complete lifecycle of a session as experienced in the Conversation UI, mapping each UI phase to the corresponding backend modules that power it.

It begins with **Session Start**, where a sales representative selects an account or creates a new session. The UI shows a loading state while backend modules create the session, fetch CRM/ERP data, load tenant configuration, and evaluate initial agent triggers.

Next is **Context Assembly**, where the Customer Context Panel is populated, Discovery Progress is initialized, and the appropriate AI agent (such as Net-New or Renewal) is selected based on trigger evaluation and account signals.

During the **Opening Move**, the AI sends a contextual greeting tailored to the customer’s situation. Quick Actions and auto-surfaced tools (like Meeting Prep Briefs or Account Overviews) appear, driven by the active agent and plugin evaluation logic.

In the **Active Conversation** phase, the rep and AI exchange messages. The system continuously updates discovery progress, surfaces recommendations, manages agent transitions, retrieves knowledge base data, and captures engagement signals.

The **Recommendation Phase** introduces product recommendations in a dedicated panel. The rep can review, accept, or dismiss them, while backend systems generate recommendations, fetch supporting product data, and log feedback signals.

During the **Action Phase**, the rep uses Quick Actions (such as generating emails or building quotes) to create deliverables. Plugins execute with full session context and access state and knowledge base APIs.

Finally, in the **Session End** phase, the rep closes or leaves the session. The system persists the session state, captures final signals, logs audit data, and ensures the session can be resumed later.

Overall, the section outlines how UI interactions and backend modules work together across the entire session lifecycle—from initiation and context building to recommendations, execution, and persistence.

nodes.title: 13.6 Module Access Map — What Module 13 Touches
nodes.summary:
Section 13.6 describes how Module 13 (M13) interacts with other backend modules through defined communication paths, data flows, and access boundaries.

M13 primarily communicates with the M1 State Engine using WebSockets for real-time updates and REST for initial synchronization, enabling bidirectional state reading and mutation through representative actions. Interaction with M2 Orchestrator, M4 Data Integration, and M5 Multi-Tenancy occurs indirectly via M1, with M13 mainly consuming state, agent responses, tenant configuration, and assembled context data.

M13 does not directly access M3 (Knowledge Base Engine); instead, knowledge access happens through backend agents and plugins. It integrates directly with M12 Plugin SDK using REST for execution and WebSockets for triggers and results, supporting bidirectional plugin interactions. Feedback is sent to M16 via REST signals, while authentication and role enforcement are handled through M18 using JWT validation on WebSocket connection and token refresh via REST.

All REST traffic flows through M20 API Gateway for routing and rate limiting. M19 Compliance passively audits state mutations by subscribing to M1 events. Overall, the document defines M13’s real-time, event-driven integration model, emphasizing indirect backend access, strict state mediation through M1, secure authentication, and controlled API routing.

structure.title: Module 14: CRM Embedded Widget
structure.prefix_summary:
# Module 14: CRM Embedded Widget

Module 14 takes the core capabilities of the Conversation UI and embeds them inside the rep’s CRM system — the application they already live in. The widget is not a miniaturized copy of Module 13; it is a purpose-built compact interface optimized for the CRM sidebar form factor. The goal: the rep should never need to leave their CRM to access platform intelligence.

nodes.title: 14.1 Supported CRM Platforms
nodes.summary:
This section outlines the CRM platforms supported in Module 14 and explains the technical integration approach for each.

It details two supported platforms: Salesforce and HubSpot. Salesforce integration is implemented as a Lightning Web Component (LWC) that renders in the Utility Bar or Record Page sidebar. It uses the LWC framework with Shadow DOM and communicates with the backend via REST-based Platform APIs, deployed as a managed package. HubSpot integration is built as a React-based iframe app that appears in the CRM record sidebar, registered through the HubSpot App Marketplace, and also communicates via REST-based Platform APIs.

The section also explains why WebSockets are not used for the CRM widget. Due to strict Content Security Policy (CSP) constraints in Salesforce and cross-origin restrictions in HubSpot iframe apps, WebSockets are difficult to implement reliably. Instead, the system uses REST with short polling (every 2–3 seconds during active sessions), which provides sufficient responsiveness for the compact sidebar widget. It further notes that Server-Sent Events (SSE) are being evaluated in the full product as a potential middle-ground solution for unidirectional push over HTTP that better aligns with CRM security policies.

nodes.title: 14.2 Auto-Context Detection
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 14.2 Auto-Context Detection

The most important capability of the CRM Widget is automatic context detection. When the rep navigates to a CRM record (Account, Opportunity, Contact), the widget automatically detects which record they’re viewing and loads the relevant session context — without the rep typing anything.

nodes.title: 14.2.1 Detection Mechanism per Platform
nodes.summary:
This section explains how the system detects CRM context on different platforms and initializes or resumes a session accordingly.

It describes platform-specific detection mechanisms:

- **Salesforce LWC** uses the Lightning Message Channel to subscribe to record page events and retrieve the `recordId` from the page context. It extracts Account, Opportunity, or Contact IDs and record type. If no record context is available (such as on a dashboard), the widget falls back to a manual account search/selection interface.

- **HubSpot Sidebar** uses the HubSpot CRM Extension SDK, which provides `context.crm.objectId` and `context.crm.objectType` when the sidebar loads. It extracts the object ID, object type (contact, company, deal), and associated company ID. If context is unavailable, it also falls back to manual account selection.

After detecting the CRM record, the widget calls the Platform API endpoint `POST /api/sessions/resolve` with CRM platform, object type, object ID, and tenant ID. The API then:
1. Maps the CRM record ID to the platform’s internal account ID using configured field mappings.
2. Checks for an existing active session for the account and sales rep.
3. Either resumes the existing session or creates a new one.

Finally, the widget loads the session state and renders the interface.

nodes.title: 14.3 Widget Interface Components
nodes.summary:
This section describes the interface components of the CRM Widget and how they differ from their full versions in Module 13. The widget is designed for a narrow sidebar (350–400px wide) and presents a streamlined, space-optimized subset of the full UI.

Key components include:

- **Mini Chat**: A compact version of the full Chat Panel with shorter message widths and collapsible AI responses. It removes inline product links and rich text formatting to save space.
- **Inline Recommendations**: Displayed as stacked cards beneath the chat, showing one card at a time with swipe or scroll navigation. Compared to the full panel, it removes side-by-side comparisons and simplifies supporting evidence to 1–2 bullet points.
- **Quick Action Chips**: A horizontally scrollable row above the chat input, limited to four visible chips with overflow handled through a “More” menu.
- **Context Summary**: A collapsible header presenting key account details such as name, health score, and top three metrics. More detailed elements like relationship maps and activity timelines are omitted since they are accessible in the main CRM.
- **Agent Badge**: A small icon and label in the header indicating the active agent. Advanced UI elements like transition animations are removed, and agent switch suggestions appear directly in chat instead of as tooltips.

Overall, the widget focuses on delivering essential functionality in a condensed format, prioritizing clarity and usability within limited screen space.

nodes.title: 14.4 CRM Write-Back
nodes.summary:
This section explains the CRM Write-Back functionality of the CRM Widget, highlighting bidirectional integration as a key differentiator from the standalone Conversation UI. It details how platform activities are automatically or manually written back into CRM records so managers and team members can track interactions without accessing the platform directly.

The document outlines specific write-back actions, including logging session activity, creating follow-up tasks, updating opportunity stages, attaching generated documents, and recording recommendation outcomes. For each action, it specifies the CRM record updated, the type of data written, and the trigger (automatic or user-initiated).

It also describes the write-back permission model, emphasizing that CRM write-back requires explicit OAuth scopes during setup and strictly respects the CRM’s existing permission model. Before any write-back occurs, a permission check is performed to ensure the user has edit access to the target record. If not, the action fails gracefully, preventing unauthorized updates and ensuring CRM security is not bypassed.

nodes.title: 14.5 Feature Parity Matrix — Module 13 vs Module 14
nodes.summary:
The document presents a feature parity comparison between Module 13 (Conversation UI) and Module 14 (CRM Widget), outlining how functionality differs due to interface constraints, embedding limitations, and CRM integration requirements.

Key points include:

- **UI and Layout Constraints:** Module 14 operates within a narrow CRM sidebar, resulting in simplified components such as limited message history (last 20 messages with load more), progress bars instead of radar charts, condensed comparison tables, and inline plugin outputs instead of a dedicated side panel.

- **Performance and Embedding Considerations:** To reduce JavaScript bundle size and comply with CRM Content Security Policy (CSP) restrictions, Module 14 replaces WebSocket real-time updates with REST polling and removes animation effects.

- **CRM-Specific Capabilities:** Unlike Module 13, Module 14 supports full CRM write-back functionality, as it is context-aware within the CRM environment.

- **Feature Reductions for Compatibility:** Keyboard shortcuts are minimized in Module 14 to avoid conflicts with the CRM’s own shortcuts.

- **Shared Limitations:** Both modules require an active internet connection and do not support offline functionality.

Overall, Module 13 provides a richer, full-featured conversation experience, while Module 14 offers a streamlined, CRM-embedded version optimized for space, security, and integration constraints.

nodes.title: 14.6 Module Access Map — What Module 14 Touches
nodes.summary:
This section describes how Module 14 (M14) integrates with and accesses other backend modules within the platform. It provides a structured access map outlining the communication paths, dependencies, and behavior across modules.

Key points covered:

- **Shared Session and State Management (M1 State Engine):** M14 interacts with the State Engine via REST APIs for reading and writing session data. Session continuity is maintained across modules (e.g., switching between M13 and M14 preserves state).

- **Agent Orchestration (M2 Orchestrator):** Access is indirect through the State Engine, ensuring consistent agent behavior regardless of the user interface surface.

- **Data Integration and CRM Mapping (M4 Data Integration):** M14 uses REST APIs to resolve CRM record IDs to platform accounts and validate write-back permissions.

- **Multi-Tenancy Support (M5 Multi-Tenancy):** Tenant configuration is accessed indirectly through session state, enabling tenant-specific branding such as logos and colors in the widget.

- **Plugin Execution (M12 Plugin SDK):** M14 executes plugins via REST APIs, with plugin outputs rendered directly within the widget interface instead of a side panel.

- **Feedback Collection (M16 Feedback Engine):** Feedback signals are sent via REST, including standard signals used by M13 and additional CRM-specific signals such as write-back completion.

- **Authentication and Authorization (M18 Auth & Roles):** Authentication occurs through an OAuth flow within a CRM iframe, with JWT-based calls to the platform. CRM SSO may integrate with platform SSO for seamless access.

- **API Routing and Rate Limiting (M20 API Gateway):** All REST requests are routed through the API Gateway, with widget traffic rate-limited separately from other modules like M13.

Overall, the document outlines M14’s reliance on REST-based communication through the Platform API, shared session state, consistent agent logic, CRM integration, tenant-aware customization, and secure, rate-limited access via the API Gateway.

structure.title: Module 15: Admin Portal
structure.prefix_summary:
# Module 15: Admin Portal

Module 15 is the administrative interface used by Sales Ops teams and platform administrators to configure, manage, and monitor the Sales Intelligence Platform. Unlike Modules 13 and 14 (which serve sales reps during customer conversations), Module 15 is a traditional web application with forms, tables, editors, and dashboards. It communicates exclusively via REST API (Platform API) and has no real-time requirements.

| Who Uses Module 15? The Admin Portal serves two personas. Sales Ops / Admin: the primary user, responsible for configuring business rules, managing the knowledge base, setting up integrations, and monitoring adoption. They access all seven admin sections. Platform Super Admin: an internal role for cross-tenant support, used by the platform vendor’s customer success team. They can view tenant configurations, run diagnostics, and assist with onboarding. This role is enforced by M18 (Auth & Roles). |
| --- |

nodes.title: 15.1 Admin Sections Overview
nodes.summary:
The document outlines the **Admin Sections Overview**, detailing key administrative modules within the system, their purposes, associated backend components, and supported CRUD operations.

It describes seven main admin areas:

- **KB Management** – Manages knowledge base documents, including uploading, editing, deleting, browsing, and maintaining product relationships. Powered by the M3 KB Engine, it supports full CRUD operations with cascade checks on deletion.

- **Integration Setup** – Handles connections to external CRM and ERP systems, including field mapping and synchronization configuration. Managed by the M4 Data Integration module, it supports full CRUD operations with data retention options upon disconnection.

- **Business Rules** – Provides a visual rule builder for tenant-specific logic, including testing and execution logs. Built on the M5 Multi-Tenancy business rules layer, it supports full CRUD operations, including rule deactivation.

- **Agent Config** – Allows configuration of workflow agents (M6–M11), such as enabling/disabling agents and setting thresholds or priorities. Managed by the M2 Orchestrator and M5 Multi-Tenancy modules, it supports read and update operations only, as agents are platform-defined.

- **User Management** – Manages users and role assignments (e.g., rep, manager, admin, executive). Powered by M18 Auth & Roles, it supports full CRUD operations, including user reassignment upon deletion.

- **Discovery Framework** – Enables customization of tenant-specific discovery dimensions and progress weights. Built on the M5 Multi-Tenancy discovery configuration layer, it supports full CRUD operations with impact analysis on deletions.

- **Usage Analytics** – Provides admin-level insights such as adoption rates, feature usage, and data quality metrics. Supported by the M17 Analytics Dashboard (admin view), it is read-only and displays aggregated metrics with filtering capabilities.

Overall, the section provides a structured overview of administrative functionalities, backend ownership, and the scope of data operations available in each module.

nodes.title: 15.2 KB Management — Deep Dive
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 15.2 KB Management — Deep Dive

The Knowledge Base Management section is the most complex admin surface. It is the interface through which tenant administrators populate M3 (KB Engine) with product information, competitive intelligence, pricing rules, and sales collateral that agents and plugins consume.

nodes.title: 15.2.1 Document Upload Pipeline
nodes.summary:
The document section describes the **Document Upload Pipeline (15.2.1)** and outlines the end-to-end workflow for uploading and publishing documents within the system. It details four main stages:

1. **Upload** – Admins upload supported file types (PDF, DOCX, XLSX, CSV, Markdown). The backend validates files through the Platform API and M3 ingestion pipeline (type, size, malware scan), while the UI displays upload progress and estimated processing time.

2. **Processing** – The system processes documents by chunking content, generating embeddings, extracting metadata (such as titles, product mentions, and categories), and updating vector and keyword indexes. The UI reflects real-time status transitions and provides clear error messages if issues occur.

3. **Review** – Admins review and edit extracted metadata, assign product tags and categories, and confirm accuracy. Backend updates metadata and recalculates graph relationships if tags are modified. The UI supports this with editable forms and auto-suggested tags.

4. **Publish** – Once approved, admins publish the document, making it accessible to agents and plugins via the KB Query API. The backend activates the document, and the UI confirms publication with visual indicators.

Overall, the section explains the structured workflow, backend processing steps, and corresponding UI feedback for managing document ingestion and availability.

nodes.title: 15.2.2 Visual Relationship Editor
nodes.summary:
The section describes the **Visual Relationship Editor**, a graph-based interface that allows administrators to define relationships between products within M3’s knowledge graph. These defined relationships directly influence how different AI agents recommend, upsell, bundle, or replace products during customer interactions.

It explains that relationships such as **complements, upgrades_to, replaces, bundles_with, and competes_with** determine specific agent behaviors. For example, complementary relationships drive cross-sell recommendations, upgrade relationships power upsell suggestions, replacement relationships guide renewal proposals, bundling relationships help construct complete solution packages, and competitive relationships support positioning against rival products.

A table outlines each relationship type, its meaning, the specific agent it impacts, and practical examples, demonstrating how structured product connections shape automated sales and recommendation strategies across the system.

nodes.title: 15.3 Integration Setup
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 15.3 Integration Setup

The Integration Setup section is where admins connect the platform to external systems (CRM, ERP) via Module 4 (Data Integration). The admin portal provides a guided wizard that walks through each step of the integration process.

nodes.title: 15.3.1 Connection Wizard Flow
nodes.summary:
The document section describes the **Connection Wizard Flow** for integrating external CRM/ERP systems into the platform, outlining both the **admin-facing steps** and the corresponding **backend processing** handled by system modules.

### Main Points Covered

1. **Platform Selection**
   - Admin selects a supported CRM/ERP (e.g., Salesforce, HubSpot, SAP, Oracle).
   - The system loads the appropriate connector template, including OAuth configuration, API endpoints, and required scopes.

2. **Authentication**
   - Admin completes an OAuth login and grants permissions.
   - The system securely stores encrypted access and refresh tokens in a tenant vault and logs the authorization event.

3. **Field Mapping**
   - Admin maps CRM/ERP fields to platform fields (e.g., “Annual Revenue” → “ARR”).
   - Field mappings are stored in tenant configuration, with default mappings pre-populated for common platforms.

4. **Sync Configuration**
   - Admin chooses sync frequency (real-time via webhooks or batch intervals) and selects objects to sync.
   - The system registers webhook endpoints or schedules batch sync jobs accordingly.

5. **Test Connection**
   - Admin tests the integration by pulling a sample record.
   - The system retrieves a sample record, applies field normalization based on mappings, and displays the result for review.

6. **Activation**
   - Admin activates the integration, triggering an initial full sync.
   - All relevant records are pulled, normalized, stored, and progress is streamed to the UI.

### Integration Health Monitoring

Once connected, the system provides a health dashboard displaying:
- Last sync time  
- Number of records synced  
- Error count  
- Average sync latency  

If issues occur (e.g., expired OAuth tokens, API rate limits, broken field mappings), the system:
- Displays amber/red health status with remediation steps  
- Sends proactive email alerts to notify admins of degraded integration health  

Overall, the section outlines a structured, secure, and monitored integration setup process with automated backend handling and proactive health management.

nodes.title: 15.4 Business Rules — Visual Rule Builder
nodes.prefix_summary:
This section explains the **Business Rules — Visual Rule Builder**, a feature that allows administrators to create tenant-specific logic without coding. These rules are stored in M5’s business_rules layer and are executed by agents during conversations. The system uses a drag-and-drop visual interface composed of condition and action blocks.

Key components include:

- **Condition Blocks (IF statements):** Define criteria based on session data, customer context, or product attributes (e.g., industry type or ARR thresholds).
- **Action Blocks (THEN statements):** Specify resulting behaviors such as modifying agent responses, filtering recommendations, requiring approvals, or sending notifications.
- **Exception Blocks (UNLESS clauses):** Override rules under specific circumstances to prevent unnecessary restrictions.
- **Priority:** Determines rule execution order when multiple rules apply, with higher-priority rules overriding conflicting lower-priority ones.
- **Scope:** Defines which agents or workflows the rule applies to or excludes.

Overall, the section outlines how admins can control agent behavior and workflow logic through configurable, prioritized, and scoped business rules.

nodes.title: 15.4.1 Test and Preview
nodes.summary:
### 15.4.1 Test and Preview

Before activating a rule, admins can test it against sample scenarios. The admin selects a test customer (from real CRM data, anonymized if needed) and a test agent workflow. The platform runs the rule evaluation and shows: which conditions matched, which actions would fire, which recommendations would be filtered/modified, and what the rep would see differently. This prevents admins from deploying rules that accidentally block all recommendations or create contradictory constraints.

nodes.title: 15.5 Agent Configuration
nodes.summary:
This section explains how tenant administrators can configure the behavior of predefined platform agents (M6–M11), even though they cannot create or delete them. Configuration is done at the tenant level and controls how agents operate within that specific environment.

Key configuration areas include:

- **Enable/Disable Agents**: Admins can control which agents are active for their tenant based on business needs.
- **Trigger Thresholds**: Adjust the sensitivity of agent activation conditions, such as confidence scores or other criteria.
- **Priority Weights**: Define which agent takes precedence when multiple agents could be triggered simultaneously.
- **Quick Action Set**: Specify which plugins (M12) are available during an agent’s workflow to tailor available actions.
- **Discovery Dimensions**: Determine which contextual or analytical dimensions an agent should focus on during its operation.

All configurations are stored in structured fields within the tenant configuration (M5), allowing fine-grained, tenant-specific customization of agent behavior.

nodes.title: 15.6 User Management
nodes.prefix_summary:
The **User Management** section defines how platform access and permissions are structured, emphasizing that it manages platform-specific roles enforced by M18 (Auth & Roles), rather than replacing the CRM’s native user management.

It outlines five primary roles, each with distinct platform access, module access, and data scope:

- **Sales Rep**: Access to conversation interfaces (M13, M14) with full conversation capabilities and enabled plugins. Data access is restricted to their own assigned accounts, enforced through role-based data scoping.
- **Sales Manager**: Includes all Sales Rep capabilities plus read-only visibility into team members’ sessions and access to team-level analytics (M17). Data scope is limited to team accounts based on CRM hierarchy synced via M4.
- **Sales Ops / Admin**: Full administrative access through the Admin Portal (M15) and operations analytics (M17). Responsible for knowledge base management, rules, integrations, user management, and agent configuration. Access is tenant-wide but restricted to their own tenant.
- **Executive**: Access limited to executive-level analytics (M17), including ROI and revenue impact dashboards. No access to conversations or individual account/session drill-down—only aggregated tenant-wide metrics.
- **Platform Super Admin**: Cross-tenant visibility via the Admin Portal for diagnostics and onboarding support. Cannot modify tenant data without explicit approval, with access governed by tenant isolation (M5) and audited break-glass controls (M19).

Overall, the section defines a clear role-based access control model with strict data scoping, tenant isolation, and separation of operational, analytical, and administrative responsibilities.

nodes.title: 15.6.1 User Onboarding Flow
nodes.summary:
### 15.6.1 User Onboarding Flow

When an admin invites a new user: admin enters the user’s email and selects a role. The Platform API creates a pending user record in M18. An invitation email is sent with a one-time setup link. The user clicks the link and authenticates via the tenant’s SSO provider (configured in M18). On first login, M4 syncs the user’s CRM profile to determine account assignments. The user’s data scope is automatically set based on CRM assignments. The admin can override account assignments manually if needed.

nodes.title: 15.7 Discovery Framework Configuration
nodes.summary:
This section explains how administrators can configure the Discovery Framework that powers the Discovery Progress component in Module 13. The framework defines the key dimensions sales reps must explore to understand a customer, and it can be tailored to different industries or tenant needs.

Admins can rename, add, or remove discovery dimensions (such as Business Challenges or Budget Authority), adjust their relative weights to influence overall completion scoring, and set custom completion thresholds per dimension to determine when discovery is considered complete. They can also assign specific dimensions to specific agents so that different roles (e.g., renewal agents) focus only on relevant areas.

Additionally, admins can customize or add the discovery questions associated with each dimension, which agents use to guide conversations and measure progress. Overall, this configuration controls what agents need to learn, how progress is calculated, and when the system shifts from discovery to recommendation mode.

nodes.title: 15.8 Usage Analytics (Admin View)
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Admin View of Usage Analytics**, which focuses on platform health, user adoption, data quality, and operational effectiveness rather than executive ROI metrics. It outlines key metric categories, their data sources, and the corresponding action triggers for administrators.

The document covers five primary metric areas:

1. **Adoption Metrics** – Tracks rep engagement, including active usage, session frequency, time spent, and feature adoption. Data is sourced from session and feedback signals, with low adoption prompting training, configuration adjustments, or feedback review.

2. **Data Quality Metrics** – Monitors knowledge base freshness, CRM sync errors, and field mapping completeness. Alerts help admins address stale content or integration issues.

3. **Agent Effectiveness Metrics** – Evaluates AI agent performance through recommendation acceptance rates, discovery completion rates, and agent switching behavior. Poor performance signals the need to refine triggers, content, or business rules.

4. **Plugin Usage Metrics** – Measures plugin execution frequency, latency, and error rates. Underused or error-prone plugins may be disabled or investigated.

5. **Compliance Metrics** – Tracks audit logs, PII detection events, and data access anomalies to ensure regulatory adherence and proper data governance.

Overall, the section defines operational metrics, their technical data sources, and actionable responses that administrators should take to maintain system effectiveness and integrity.

nodes.title: 15.9 Module Access Map — What Module 15 Touches
nodes.summary:
The document section **“15.9 Module Access Map — What Module 15 Touches”** outlines how Module 15 (the Admin Module) interacts with various backend system modules. It provides a structured mapping of which admin sections access specific backend modules, what operations are performed, and how communication occurs.

### Main Points Covered:

1. **Centralized Admin Access to Core Modules**  
   Module 15 connects to multiple backend services, acting as an administrative control layer across orchestration, knowledge management, integrations, analytics, authentication, compliance, and multi-tenancy systems.

2. **CRUD and Configuration Capabilities**  
   - Full CRUD operations are supported for modules like:
     - **M3 KB Engine** (document and relationship management)
     - **M18 Auth & Roles** (user and role management)
     - **M4 Data Integration** (CRM/ERP connections and sync configuration)
   - Configuration updates are supported for:
     - **M2 Orchestrator** (agent triggers and priorities)
     - **M5 Multi-Tenancy** (tenant-level business and agent configurations)

3. **Read-Only Access for Analytics and Compliance**  
   Some modules provide strictly read-only data access:
     - **M16 Feedback Engine** (feedback and adoption metrics)
     - **M17 Analytics Dashboard** (admin analytics views)
     - **M19 Compliance** (audit logs, PII events, access logs)

4. **Integration and Authentication Handling**  
   - External integrations use REST APIs and OAuth callback handlers.
   - Authentication, SSO configuration, and role management are handled through the Auth & Roles module.

5. **Standardized Communication Architecture**  
   - All modules communicate via **REST through the Platform API**.
   - **M20 API Gateway** routes all requests, enforcing rate limiting and authentication.
   - Multipart uploads are used where needed (e.g., document uploads to the KB Engine).

Overall, the section defines Module 15 as an administrative orchestration layer that interfaces with multiple backend systems through standardized REST-based communication, supporting a mix of configuration, management, analytics, and compliance operations.

structure.title: Shared Backend Services
structure.prefix_summary:
# Shared Backend Services

All three interface modules communicate with the backend through a shared service layer. Understanding these services clarifies how M13, M14, and M15 connect to the rest of the platform.

nodes.title: Shared.1 Platform API
nodes.summary:
The partial document describes the **Shared.1 Platform API**, a unified REST API that supports all interface modules. The API is implemented behind **Module 20 (API Gateway)**, which is responsible for rate limiting, JWT authentication validation, request routing, and response caching. All HTTP requests from modules M13, M14, and M15 pass through the API Gateway before reaching backend services.

The document outlines key API domains, their consumers, main endpoints, and authentication requirements:

- **Sessions (M13, M14)**: Handles session lifecycle and messaging, including session creation, state synchronization, message sending, and CRM context resolution. Requires rep-scoped JWT authentication.
- **Plugins (M13, M14)**: Supports plugin execution and listing available plugins per session. Access is controlled via rep-scoped JWTs and validated against tenant configuration.
- **Feedback (M13, M14)**: Allows recording feedback signals, secured with rep-scoped JWTs.
- **Knowledge Base (M15)**: Provides document management and relationship graph editing capabilities (CRUD operations). Requires admin-scoped JWTs.
- **Integrations (M15)**: Manages external system connections, including creation, configuration updates, and connection testing. Requires admin-scoped JWTs.
- **Tenant Configuration (M15)**: Enables reading and updating business rules, agent configurations, and discovery framework settings. Requires admin-scoped JWTs.
- **Users (M15)**: Supports user management functions such as inviting users, listing users, updating roles, and removing users. Requires admin-scoped JWTs.
- **Analytics (M15, M17)**: Provides endpoints for adoption, effectiveness, plugin usage, and compliance analytics. Accessible with admin- or executive-scoped JWTs.

Overall, the document defines the structure, responsibilities, endpoint coverage, and role-based authentication model of the centralized Platform API.

nodes.title: Shared.2 WebSocket Service
nodes.summary:
The document describes the Shared.2 WebSocket Service, a dedicated real-time communication layer used exclusively by the Conversation UI (Module 13). It maintains persistent connections with active representative sessions and delivers state updates from the State Engine (M1). The service listens to M1’s event bus and routes broadcasted changes to the correct client based on session identifiers.

Key implementation aspects include:

- **Scaling:** Because WebSocket connections are stateful, horizontal scaling relies on sticky sessions with Redis-backed session affinity. If a server fails, clients automatically reconnect and perform a full state synchronization.
- **Authentication:** JWT tokens are validated during the WebSocket upgrade. Token refresh occurs through a separate REST endpoint, with refreshed tokens sent via a special WebSocket message. Expired tokens result in the connection closing with a specific auth_expired code.
- **Message Ordering:** Each message carries a monotonically increasing per-session sequence number. Clients detect gaps and request a full state re-sync to ensure consistency and recover from missed events.
- **Backpressure Handling:** The server buffers up to 100 unacknowledged messages for slow clients. If this limit is exceeded, intermediate updates are dropped and replaced with a full state snapshot once the client catches up.
- **Multi-Tab Support:** Multiple browser tabs connected to the same session receive identical events. Updates made in one tab are reflected in others via shared session state in M1, supporting concurrent tab usage by representatives.

Overall, the document outlines the architecture and reliability mechanisms of the WebSocket Service, focusing on real-time delivery, scalability, authentication, consistency, and resilience.

nodes.title: Shared.3 Auth Service
nodes.summary:
The document describes the **Shared.3 Auth Service**, which wraps the platform’s Auth & Roles module and provides centralized authentication and authorization across all interface modules. Regardless of how users authenticate, each flow results in a JWT that the Platform API validates.

It outlines authentication flows, token contents, and session durations for three modules:

- **M13 (Conversation UI):** Uses standard SSO via the tenant’s identity provider (e.g., Okta, Azure AD). After SAML/OIDC authentication, a JWT is issued containing tenant ID, user ID, role, and account scope. Sessions typically last 8 hours with refresh token support.

- **M14 (CRM Widget):** Uses chained SSO, leveraging the existing CRM session for silent token exchange. If the exchange fails, a one-click login is offered. The JWT includes tenant ID, user ID, role, CRM platform, and CRM user ID. Session duration matches the CRM session.

- **M15 (Admin Portal):** Uses standard SSO with mandatory MFA and step-up authentication for admin roles. Tokens include tenant ID, user ID, role, and permissions. Sessions are shorter (4 hours) with required re-authentication for sensitive actions.

Overall, the document explains how different modules authenticate users, what information their tokens contain, and how session management varies based on security needs.

structure.title: Cross-Module Interaction Summary
structure.summary:
The document provides a consolidated overview of how backend modules (M1–M20) interact with three frontend interface modules: M13 (Conversation UI), M14 (CRM Widget), and M15 (Admin Portal). It serves as a definitive reference for mapping backend capabilities to UI surfaces.

Key points covered:

- **Core Runtime & State Management:** M1 (State Engine) is the primary integration point for the Conversation UI via WebSocket and for the CRM Widget via REST polling, while the Admin Portal has no direct access.
- **Agent & Orchestration Layer:** M2 (Orchestrator) and M6–M11 (Agents) are consumed indirectly by user-facing interfaces through state events, with administrative configuration handled in the Admin Portal.
- **Knowledge & Data Systems:** M3 (Knowledge Base Engine) and M4 (Data Integration) support runtime operations indirectly for end-user interfaces, while the Admin Portal provides full CRUD management and integration setup capabilities.
- **Multi-Tenancy & Configuration:** M5 governs tenant-specific configuration, accessed indirectly by user interfaces and directly managed within various Admin Portal sections.
- **Plugin & Feedback Systems:** M12 (Plugin SDK) is directly used by both user interfaces for execution, while M16 (Feedback Engine) is directly integrated for feedback submission, with analytics visibility in the Admin Portal.
- **Analytics & Compliance:** M17 (Analytics Dashboard) and M19 (Compliance) are accessible only through read-only administrative views.
- **Authentication & Security:** M18 (Auth & Roles) manages JWT validation, SSO, role-based access, and step-up authentication across modules.
- **API Gateway:** M20 routes all REST traffic for all interface modules.

Overall, the document clarifies which backend modules are accessed directly, indirectly, or administratively, and distinguishes runtime consumption from configuration and oversight responsibilities.

structure.title: Key Technical Decisions Summary
structure.summary:
The partial document summarizes key technical decisions made across multiple modules (M13, M14, M15, and shared infrastructure), outlining the chosen approaches, the reasoning behind them, and alternatives that were considered but rejected.

Main points covered:

1. Transport Protocol Decisions by Module  
   - M13 uses WebSocket for real-time communication (for sub-second conversational updates) and REST for initial synchronization. REST polling was rejected due to latency and load concerns.  
   - M14 uses REST with short polling (2–3 seconds) because CRM Content Security Policy (CSP) restrictions make WebSockets unreliable. WebSockets and Server-Sent Events (SSE) were considered but rejected due to platform limitations.  
   - M15 uses REST only, as it handles admin-style request-response operations that do not require real-time communication.

2. CRM Context Detection (M14)  
   - Platform-specific SDKs (e.g., Lightning Message Channel, HubSpot CRM SDK) are used to detect record context.  
   - URL parsing was rejected because it is fragile and prone to breaking when CRM URL structures change.

3. State Management Strategy (M13)  
   - A server-authoritative model (via M1) is used, with the UI acting as a projection.  
   - This supports session resumability, multi-tab usage, and prevents state drift.  
   - Client-side state with synchronization was rejected due to the complexity of conflict resolution.

4. CRM Write-Back Security (M14)  
   - All write operations are permission-checked through M4 before execution.  
   - This ensures alignment with the CRM’s native security model and avoids audit risks.  
   - Relying solely on platform permissions was rejected due to potential compliance and auditing concerns.

5. Rule Testing Approach (M15)  
   - Rule testing is performed against real (anonymized) customer data to ensure realistic outcomes.  
   - Synthetic test data was rejected because it does not adequately reflect real production scenarios.

6. Shared API Gateway Architecture  
   - A single shared API gateway (M20) is used for all interface modules.  
   - This provides consistent rate limiting, authentication, and observability.  
   - Per-module gateways were rejected due to operational overhead and policy inconsistencies.

Overall, the document emphasizes reliability, security, operational consistency, and platform constraints as primary drivers behind the architectural and technical decisions.
